History:
- Chief complaint: Painful, dry, cracked skin on palms with intermittent itch.
- Onset/duration: Began ~3–4 months ago; worsened recently.
- Progression/impact: Pain now significant; unable to work; off work for past 3 days.
- Location: Palms primarily; mild generalized dryness on legs (not severe).
- Triggers/exposures: Works as a hotel housekeeper; frequent exposure to cleaning products; inconsistent glove use; job change ~4 months ago.
- Associated symptoms: Itch intermittent; bleeding occurs only when scratched; denies fever, nausea/vomiting, bowel or urinary symptoms; appetite well-maintained.
- Prior treatments: E45 emollient and an antihistamine (name not documented) without benefit.

Past Medical History:
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
- No known prior eczema/dermatitis.
- Medications: Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Allergies: No known drug or general allergies.
- Family history: Diabetes; no known skin disease; no asthma or bowel disorders reported.
- Social: Housekeeper in a hotel; non-smoker; alcohol a couple of pints per week.

Physical Examination:
- No in-person exam documented (teleconsult).
- Patient-reported findings: Dry, cracked palmar skin; painful; intermittently itchy; bleeding only when scratched; no spontaneous bleeding.
- Negative/systemic: No fever; no GI or GU complaints; otherwise feels well.
- No documentation of erythema, swelling, discharge, or signs of infection.

Impression:
- Likely irritant contact dermatitis of the palms related to occupational exposure to cleaning agents.

Management Plan:
- Avoid triggers: Wear protective gloves consistently during all cleaning tasks.
- Topical corticosteroid for inflamed areas (specific agent/dose/frequency not documented).
- Strong emollients: Apply generously 3–4 times daily for the next couple of weeks.
- Prescription sent to patient’s pharmacy.
- Follow-up: If not improved within 10–14 days, return for reassessment; return sooner if symptoms worsen or spread.

Patient Summary:
- 45-year-old woman with 3–4 months of painful, itchy, cracked palmar skin, acutely worse and affecting work. Occupational exposure to cleaning chemicals without consistent glove use suggests irritant contact dermatitis. Plan includes protective measures, topical steroid, and frequent emollients with close follow-up.

Key Takeaways:
- Wear gloves at all times when using cleaning products.
- Use emollients 3–4 times daily and apply the prescribed steroid to inflamed areas.
- Seek care sooner if worsening or spreading; otherwise reassess if not improved in 10–14 days.

Next Steps:
- Monitor response over 10–14 days.
- If persistent or worsening at follow-up, clinician to consider alternative therapies or further evaluation (details not documented).

Quality checks:
- Missing elements: No vitals; no direct skin examination or photos; no detailed description of lesions (erythema, scaling, fissures); metformin dose/route/frequency not documented; specific steroid and emollient names/strengths and instructions not documented; no documentation of diabetes control or medication reconciliation beyond metformin.
- Internal conflicts: Patient initially denied bleeding, later reported bleeding only when scratching (conflict noted).
- Transcript quality: Some incomplete/inaudible segments; overall history adequate for provisional diagnosis.
